statement: A mandatory registry of large training clusters (or chip-location tracking) operates in >= 2 of the top-3 jurisdictions (official gazettes; by 2028-12-31)
status_at_phase_end: Not met; zero of top-3. Bloc A's outgoing administration issued an export rule (Jan 2025) with data-centre authorisation and reporting elements, but its successor rescinded it before compliance began (May 2025). Bills mandating location verification for export-controlled AI chips were introduced in both chambers (May 2025) but not enacted. Bloc B took the opposite line: its cyberspace regulator summoned the leading Bloc A chip vendor over alleged tracking and remote-shutdown features (Jul 2025), treating chip-location tracking as a security threat. Neither bloc ran a mandatory domestic cluster registry.

items.summary: Bloc A's outgoing administration published a global AI-chip export framework with country tiers, compute caps, and a validated-end-user programme for data centres with security and reporting conditions. These were partial cluster-oversight elements, with compliance due mid-May 2025.
items.detail: BIS Interim Final Rule 'Framework for Artificial Intelligence Diffusion' (90 FR 4544, 2025-01-15), incl. Data Center VEU and controls on closed model weights >1e26 FLOP.

items.summary: A bill introduced in Bloc A's upper chamber would require location-verification mechanisms on export-controlled AI chips within 180 days of enactment, plus diversion and tampering reporting, and would let the commerce ministry keep a record of each chip's location and end user. A companion bill followed on 2025-05-15. Neither was enacted in 2025.
items.detail: Chip Security Act, S.1705 (Sen. Cotton, introduced 2025-05-08; referred to Banking Committee) and House companion (Reps. Foster, Huizenga, Moolenaar, Krishnamoorthi, 2025-05-15). Status at end-2025: introduced.

items.summary: Bloc A's commerce department rescinded the January chip-export framework two days before compliance and promised a replacement rule. It instead issued anti-diversion guidance and added licence requirements for two Southeast Asian transit markets.
items.detail: BIS press release 2025-05-13 (verified via search snippet): rescission of AI Diffusion Rule; guidance on Huawei Ascend, diversion red flags; licensing for Bloc I and Bloc J.

items.summary: Bloc A's national AI action plan recommended exploring location-verification features on advanced chips and stronger end-use monitoring against diversion. It was a policy recommendation, not a mandate.
items.detail: 'Bloc A's AI Action Plan' (White House, 2025-07-23), section on export-control enforcement ('explore leveraging new and existing location verification features'). Wording recalled, not re-verified in this run.

items.summary: Bloc B's cyberspace regulator summoned the leading Bloc A AI-chip vendor to explain alleged 'backdoor' risks (tracking, positioning, remote shutdown) in chips sold into Bloc B, citing Bloc A legislative proposals for mandatory tracking. The vendor denied any backdoors. This signals that Bloc B will resist foreign chip-location tracking.
items.detail: CAC statement 2025-07-31 (cac.gov.cn/2025-07/31/c_1755675743897163.htm) on Nvidia H20; CNBC/SCMP/NYT 2025-07-31.

items.summary: No mandatory registry of large training clusters and no chip-location-tracking mandate was in force in any top-3 compute jurisdiction at end-2025. Bloc B's domestic compute-network schemes are not a public mandatory cluster registry (not systematically checked).
items.detail: Checked: Federal Register/BIS, Congress.gov, CAC. Third top-3 jurisdiction not separately checked.
